blocks.title: Damped oscillations
blocks.text: Oscillations whose amplitude decreases because of resistive forces are called damped oscillations, and the resistive forces are called damping forces.

In an ideal free oscillation the total mechanical energy stays constant, as for the mass-spring system, a body moving in a circle and a simple pendulum. In practice, dissipating forces such as air resistance and friction act, so the amplitude decreases gradually with time and the body finally comes to rest. For example, a girl on a swing oscillates with smaller and smaller amplitude and eventually stops (Fig 14.14); the damped oscillation is shown on a graph in Fig 14.15. A swinging pendulum slowly coming to rest, and an oscillating tuning fork touched with a finger, are other examples.

blocks.alt: Two moments of a girl on a playground swing with no one pushing: the swing moves back and forth on its own and slowly comes to rest.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.14: Damped oscillation of swing (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.14).

blocks.alt: Displacement against time from O. The curve oscillates about the time axis, and each swing is smaller than the one before; two dashed curves above and below form a narrowing envelope.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.15: Graphical representation of damped oscillation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.15).

items: Light damping: the energy and amplitude decrease gradually. A playground swing is a good example.
Heavy damping: the body takes a long time to return to rest, for example a pendulum in thick oil.
Critical damping: the body returns to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time, for example the shock absorbers of a car.

blocks.text: Shock absorbers in the suspension system of a car are a practical application of damping. Damping is needed for a comfortable ride when a car moves on a bumpy, rough road: without it the car would keep bouncing after every bump.

blocks.alt: A car wheel joined to the body by suspension arms and a shock absorber with a coil spring wound round it.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.16: Suspension system of a vehicle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.16).
